strengths: Well-motivated problem reframing from text generation to evidence-centric planning, with clear articulation of limitations in prior approaches
Solid architectural design with multi-agent decomposition and explicit intermediate artifacts that enhance transparency
Valuable benchmark contribution (RebuttalBench with 9.3K samples) using clever follow-up reviewer signals as ground truth
Appropriate evaluation rubric focusing on relevance, argumentation quality, and communication rather than fluency alone
Consistent experimental improvements across all metrics and multiple LLM backbones, with meaningful ablations showing evidence construction as most critical component
Insightful finding that weaker base models benefit more from the framework, suggesting task decomposition compensates for limited model capacity
Concrete case studies in Appendix E effectively demonstrate advantages of structured planning over direct generation
weaknesses: Evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-judge with no human validation or correlation to actual reviewer satisfaction—the core claims lack human evidence

Critical HITL component presented as central feature is explicitly unevaluated due to batch evaluation constraints; reported results called 'conservative lower bound' but no data showing HITL improvement
Very limited scale for generalization: only 20 papers in Challenge set; all evaluation on ICLR with no assessment on other venues or fields
Ground truth using follow-up reviewer comments is indirect proxy; positive follow-up does not guarantee objectively good rebuttal; no comparison to papers with known acceptance/rejection outcomes
Weak baseline comparisons: chat-LLM baseline described but not empirically tested; no comparison to simpler structured prompting alternatives or human-written rebuttals

Reproducibility concerns: code not provided; heavy reliance on proprietary LLM APIs; key technical details underspecified (concern extraction mechanisms, consistency checker formalization, external evidence source limitations)
No analysis of failure modes, error propagation through pipeline, or computational cost-benefit analysis relative to simpler alternatives
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, significance tests, or cross-validation; no inter-rater agreement reported for LLM judge; no validation that 0-5 rubric correlates with downstream measures
Practical deployment concerns unaddressed: latency, API costs, integration with real rebuttal workflows under time constraints unclear
Hybrid context construction underspecified for concerns spanning multiple sections or addressing global properties

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing approaches (hallucination, missed concerns, opacity)
Rigorous evaluation methodology including human annotation study (100% accuracy on outcome classification), author-centric preference study (τ=0.646), and cross-model robustness checks
Thoughtfully designed multi-agent architecture with explicit verification checkpoints and evidence-linking that addresses real failure modes
Valuable benchmark contribution (RebuttalBench) with careful data filtering through outcome-based classification and confidence stratification
Insightful qualitative analysis, particularly the 'Coverage Paradox' showing how removing verification produces worse responses despite higher coverage scores
Consistent empirical improvements across all models and dimensions, with larger gains for weaker models (GPT-5-mini +0.55 avg vs. Gemini-3-Flash +0.33)
Comprehensive ablation studies cleanly isolating component contributions, with Evidence Construction identified as most critical
Full reproducibility support via prompt templates in appendices and careful experimental documentation
Thoughtful ethical considerations addressing misuse risks, hallucination prevention, and privacy concerns
weaknesses: Critical validation gap: HITL (human-in-the-loop) is presented as core contribution, but all results are from fully automated mode with no empirical validation of HITL effectiveness; results are thus 'conservative lower bounds' that cannot validate central claims about transparency and author control
Modest empirical improvements that don't strongly justify system complexity: Relevance +0.68-0.78 (~13-16%), Communication Quality +0.23-0.32; improvements are consistent but incremental

Severely limited evaluation scope: RebuttalBench-Challenge contains only 20 papers and 106 multi-turn cases; data restricted to ICLR 2023 with no evaluation on other venues, limiting generalization claims

Core concern extraction not independently validated: while ablation shows −0.17 semantic alignment when removed, there is no direct evaluation of extraction precision/recall versus human-identified concerns
External evidence retrieval is basic: uses only arXiv API, no evaluation of retrieval quality, no analysis of whether retrieved papers are effectively used in rebuttals
No real-world validation: no user study with actual authors, no measurement of cognitive burden reduction, no evidence authors accept/modify proposed plans

LLM-as-judge limitations inadequately addressed: while cross-model robustness is checked, known biases in LLM evaluation remain; human preference study has only 9 participants with moderate correlation (τ=0.646)
Missing computational analysis: no latency/cost comparison between RebuttalAgent and direct prompting; multi-step pipeline overhead not quantified
Action items insufficiently analyzed: central to preventing hallucination but sparse evaluation; only anecdotal case studies, no comparison of action item quality with baselines
Limited methodological novelty: system primarily combines existing techniques (compression, RAG, planning) without advancing fundamental NLP/NLG methods
Reproducibility gaps: code not released, exact arXiv retrieval logic unspecified, some filtering definitions vague (e.g., 'mixed emotions')
Generalization concerns underexplored: system heavily tailored to academic peer review; unclear how it transfers to other venues, fields, or non-English reviews
